topic: working a restored canal lock: gate mitre, rubbish on the cill, paddle gear and the balance beam

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-4)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: level recorder na pound powyzej sluzy; referent zwyczajny procesowy zakotwiczony poza rozmowa

base: I look after a restored lock on our canal and the chamber empties itself overnight.
The upper lock in the same flight holds its water for days on end.
A level recorder on the pound above notes the water height every single hour.
Water runs visibly through the lower gates even when both paddles are fully down.
Is that the gates failing to mitre, or the paddles seating badly in their frames?
Start with the mitre, since a gate that will not close tight leaks everywhere.
Push both gates shut by hand and look along the joint where they meet.
A gap at the top usually means silt or rubbish caught on the cill.
Paddles are the second suspect and their leaks sound quite different from gate leaks.
The gates meet cleanly at the top but stand apart near the bottom.
Something solid seems to be lying on the cill under the mitre post.
The level recorder shows the pound dropping about four inches through each night.
Can I clear the cill without draining the whole chamber down to the invert?
You can often clear it with a rake worked along the cill from above.
Drop the water to the lower level first so the gates hang free.
A branch or a lost fender is the usual find on a cill.
Rake it clear, then close the gates and watch the joint from the walkway.
A waterlogged fence post came off the cill and the gates now meet properly.
The chamber still loses water, though far more slowly than it did before.
The upper lock has newer paddle gear, with rubber seals around each frame.
Would seals like those cure the rest, or is my timber gear worth keeping?
Keep the timber gear, because it is repairable and outlasts rubber by many years.
Lift each paddle right out and look at the face that beds against the frame.
Worn timber can be planed true and packed out with a thin strip.
Grease the spindles at the same time, while the gear is already apart.
Both paddles were dished across the face and one had a split corner.
I planed them true and the chamber now holds its level all night.
The gear feels very heavy to wind, especially on the lower paddles.
Is that simply the water pressure, or should the gear run more freely?
Lower paddles are always heavy, since the whole head of water sits on them.
Even so, the rack should climb smoothly without any grinding or sudden jumps.
Grinding means the pinion teeth are worn or the rack sits out of line.
Crack the paddle open an inch first and let the pressure equalise briefly.
Cracking them open first has made the winding far easier on both sides.
Boats now pass through in about ten minutes rather than twenty five.
The lower gates still swing shut on their own when the chamber fills.
Is that swing dangerous for crews, or is it perfectly normal behaviour?
Gates that swing shut are normal and most old locks were built that way.
The heel post leans very slightly, so the gate closes under its own weight.
Warn crews to keep hands clear of the balance beam while water moves.
Grease the heel and collar each spring and the swing will stay gentle.
